newsitem.title: USA: Fed seen erring on side of growth in rate decision.
newsitem.headline: Fed seen erring on side of growth in rate decision.

text.p: The Federal Reserve's decision this week to keep interest rates steady shows it is willing to err on the side of growth as it seeks to determine if new forces in the economy are holding inflation down.
"Clearly, there are structural changes in the economy that have made it more unclear as to how to conduct monetary policy," said Ryan Krueger of Krueger Washington Research.
"There is a sense that we may be in a new era where inflation is lower and where you can have wage increases without necessarily seeing higher inflation," he added.
Following a meeting Tuesday of the central bank's Federal Open Market Committee, the Fed chose not to raise rates.

The decision stunned many economists who believe recent robust growth and a 5.1 percent unemployment rate were a recipe for higher inflation. It also stirred talk that, with the presidential election just six weeks away, a desire to stay out of the political fray may have kept the Fed on hold.

"Since it was a close call I think the election may have been a factor in the decision," said Lawrence Chimerine, managing director at the Economic Strategy Institute. More important, though, was the desire by many at the Fed to test whether its old rules on inflation still apply, he said.

Analysts widely believe Tuesday's meeting was one of the more contentious ones in recent history, particularly in light of the disclosure that eight of the 12 regional Fed banks had submitted requests for discount rate increases.

Former Fed Vice Chairman Preston Martin said discussion of theories about growth and inflation probably dominated the debate with Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan emerging as the pivotal figure in tilting a majority of the FOMC toward steady policy.
Given Greenspan's abilities as a consensus-builder, Martin said that, in the end, "I'll bet you there were only two or three dissenting votes."
A key subject of debate among economists inside and outside the Fed concerns the relationship between unemployment and inflation.

Until recently, many experts viewed a 6 percent jobless rate as the so-called "non-accelerating inflation rate of unemployment" (NAIRU) -- the lowest level of unemployment that can be sustained without causing wage pressures and, ultimately, higher inflation.
After the jobless rate has stayed below 6 percent for more than two years without a noticeable price pickup, many experts believe the NAIRU has fallen but they differ on how low it is.

Still, with the unemployment rate now at a seven-year low of 5.1 percent and amid signs that wages are beginning to head higher, economists believe the Fed is testing the limits of noninflationary growth by not raising rates.

"They are taking a small risk at this point," said economist Daniel Bachman of the WEFA Group. "Looking at the labor market right now there is a little bit of a reason to believe that the Fed might be behind the curve (on fighting inflation)."

Still, Bachman said he thinks the Fed made the right call in not raising rates, particularly because he is predicting that the economy is set to slow after booming at a 4.8 percent rate in the second quarter.
"There were some very good arguments on the side of the people on the FOMC who didn't see evidence that inflation was going to pick up," said chief economist James Annable of First Chicago NBD.
"I think (the lack of a rate rise) is a rather healthy sign that the Federal Reserve is looking closely to see how this economy is working and if its old rules have changed."
